lines.text: A lake town of churches, five centuries under the Ottomans, a city shaken to the ground and a new name. This is the story of North Macedonia.
On the shore of its lake, Ohrid is one of the oldest towns in Europe, filled with churches and a World Heritage Site.
In the eight hundreds, Saint Clement taught Slavic letters at Ohrid, making it a great centre of Slavic learning.
Through five centuries of Ottoman rule the land waited, until in 1903 it rose in the Ilinden Uprising, which was crushed.
In 1910 a girl was born in Skopje who became Mother Teresa, caring for the poor and dying of Kolkata, and later named a saint.
Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova, born in 1953, would become the country's first woman president.
In the summer of 1963 an earthquake destroyed most of Skopje, and the capital had to be rebuilt almost from nothing.
Goran Pandev, born in 1983, would score at the country's first European Championship, in 2021.
In 1991, as Yugoslavia broke apart, the republic became independent, and it did so without a war.
Ten years later fighting broke out with Albanian rebels. The Ohrid Agreement ended it and gave Albanians more rights.
In 2018 the Prespa agreement with Greece settled a long dispute, and the country took the name North Macedonia.
With the dispute behind it, North Macedonia joined NATO in 2020.
And in March 2025 a fire at a nightclub in Kocani killed sixty-two people, a grief felt across the nation.
From ancient Ohrid to a new name, North Macedonia's story goes on.
